task: Chemistry internal assessment: investigate how the storage temperature of orange juice affects its ascorbic acid concentration, measured by iodate titration.
text:
The effect of storage temperature on the ascorbic acid content of orange juice, determined by redox titration with potassium iodate

Research question

How does the storage temperature of freshly squeezed orange juice (4, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C, each controlled to ± 0.5 °C) over seven days affect its ascorbic acid concentration, measured by redox titration with potassium iodate solution, and what activation energy for ascorbic acid loss does this suggest?

Background and personal engagement

I became interested in this after noticing that the juice my family leaves on the kitchen counter in summer tastes flat within days, while juice from the fridge stays fresh. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C, M = 176.12 g mol-1) is a water-soluble antioxidant that is oxidised to dehydroascorbic acid, and then irreversibly hydrolysed, when the juice is exposed to oxygen. Fresh orange juice contains roughly 400 to 500 mg dm-3, so it is a useful marker of how much nutritional value a juice keeps.

Rate of a chemical reaction increases with temperature because a larger fraction of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. The Arrhenius equation, ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT), predicts that a graph of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient -Ea/R. If I treat the loss of ascorbic acid as a first-order process, which many food chemistry studies do (for example Burdurlu et al., 2006, on citrus juice concentrates), then k can be found from the fraction of ascorbic acid remaining after a fixed time: ln(c0/c) = kt. I chose this approach because I could not measure concentration continuously, but I could measure it at the start and after seven days at each temperature.

Hypothesis: the ascorbic acid concentration will fall as storage temperature rises, and ln k will be linearly related to 1/T, giving an activation energy in the range reported for citrus juices (roughly 40 to 60 kJ mol-1).

Variables

Independent variable: storage temperature of the juice: 4, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C, set using a refrigerator, a laboratory at 20 °C, and three thermostatted water baths, each checked with a digital thermometer (± 0.5 °C).
Dependent variable: ascorbic acid concentration after 7 days, found from the titre of 0.00100 mol dm-3 potassium iodate.
Controlled variables: one batch of juice (all oranges from one bag, squeezed once, filtered through muslin, then mixed so every sample started identical); 100 cm3 of juice in each sealed 250 cm3 conical flask so the headspace of air is the same; storage in the dark (flasks wrapped in aluminium foil) because light also degrades ascorbic acid; the same 25.00 cm3 aliquot, the same mass of potassium iodide, the same volume of acid and starch in each titration; titrating within one hour of removing each flask from storage and allowing it to reach room temperature in a closed flask first.

Materials and method

Potassium iodate solution was made by dissolving 0.2140 g KIO3 (M = 214.00 g mol-1, balance ± 0.0001 g) in distilled water in a 1000.0 cm3 volumetric flask (± 0.4 cm3) giving 0.001000 mol dm-3. I used iodate in an acidified iodide solution because the iodine it generates oxidises ascorbic acid rapidly and quantitatively, and the iodate solution is a stable primary standard, unlike iodine which is volatile. The equations are:
IO3- + 5I- + 6H+ -> 3I2 + 3H2O
C6H8O6 + I2 -> C6H6O6 + 2I- + 2H+
so 1 mol of iodate corresponds to 3 mol of ascorbic acid.

For each titration I pipetted 25.00 cm3 of juice (class B pipette, ± 0.06 cm3) into a conical flask, added 1 g potassium iodide, 5 cm3 of 1.0 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid (measuring cylinder) and 1 cm3 of 1% starch solution, and titrated with the iodate from a 50.00 cm3 burette (± 0.05 cm3 per reading) until the first permanent blue-black colour. A preliminary rough titration showed the end point was near 20 cm3, so I added iodate dropwise in the last 2 cm3. Each temperature was done in triplicate, from three separate 25.00 cm3 samples of the same stored flask. I also titrated the fresh juice on day 0 as a reference value, c0.

Safety and ethics: sulfuric acid at this concentration is an irritant, so eye protection and gloves were worn. Juice was not consumed. Waste containing iodine was diluted and disposed of down the sink with plenty of water, as allowed by school guidance. No living organisms were used.

Raw data (volume of 0.001000 mol dm-3 KIO3, uncertainty of each titre ± 0.10 cm3 from two burette readings)

Day 0 (fresh): 20.8 cm3, 20.9 cm3, 21.0 cm3
4 °C: 19.7 cm3, 19.9 cm3, 19.8 cm3
20 °C: 16.8 cm3, 17.0 cm3, 16.9 cm3
30 °C: 14.1 cm3, 14.3 cm3, 14.2 cm3
40 °C: 10.7 cm3, 10.9 cm3, 10.8 cm3
50 °C: 7.4 cm3, 7.6 cm3, 7.5 cm3

Qualitative observations: the juice at 50 °C had visibly darkened to a brownish colour and smelled different; the 4 °C juice looked unchanged. The end point was easiest to see in the pale 4 °C samples, and harder to judge in the darker 50 °C samples.

Data processing

Sample calculation for 20 °C, mean titre 16.9 cm3:
n(IO3-) = 0.001000 x 0.0169 = 1.69 x 10-5 mol
n(ascorbic acid) = 3 x 1.69 x 10-5 = 5.07 x 10-5 mol in 25.00 cm3
c = 5.07 x 10-5 / 0.02500 = 2.03 x 10-3 mol dm-3 = 0.357 g dm-3 = 357 mg dm-3.

Uncertainty: titre percentage uncertainty 0.10/16.9 = 0.6%, pipette 0.06/25.00 = 0.24%, KIO3 concentration about 0.1%, giving about 0.9% in total, or ± 3 mg dm-3. The spread of the three trials (range 0.2 cm3, so ± 0.1 cm3) is the same size as the burette uncertainty, so I used the larger of the two. For the lowest titre (7.5 cm3) the uncertainty is 1.6%, ± 3 mg dm-3.

Mean results:
Day 0: titre 20.9 ± 0.1 cm3, c0 = 442 ± 4 mg dm-3
4 °C: 19.8 ± 0.1 cm3, c = 418 ± 4 mg dm-3, loss 5.3%
20 °C: 16.9 ± 0.1 cm3, c = 357 ± 4 mg dm-3, loss 19.1%
30 °C: 14.2 ± 0.1 cm3, c = 300 ± 3 mg dm-3, loss 32.1%
40 °C: 10.8 ± 0.1 cm3, c = 228 ± 3 mg dm-3, loss 48.3%
50 °C: 7.5 ± 0.1 cm3, c = 159 ± 3 mg dm-3, loss 64.1%

Figure 1: scatter graph of ascorbic acid concentration (mg dm-3, y-axis) against storage temperature (°C, x-axis) with vertical error bars of ± 3 to 4 mg dm-3 (they are barely larger than the markers) and a straight line of best fit with gradient -5.7 mg dm-3 per °C and R2 = 0.98. The line is a good fit but the 4 °C and 50 °C points are slightly above it and the 30 to 40 °C points slightly below, suggesting gentle curvature.

Assuming first-order loss over t = 7 days, I calculated k = ln(c0/c)/7 in day-1:
4 °C (277.15 K): k = 0.0077 day-1; 1/T = 3.608 x 10-3 K-1; ln k = -4.87
20 °C (293.15 K): k = 0.0303 day-1; 1/T = 3.411 x 10-3 K-1; ln k = -3.50
30 °C (303.15 K): k = 0.0552 day-1; 1/T = 3.299 x 10-3 K-1; ln k = -2.90
40 °C (313.15 K): k = 0.0943 day-1; 1/T = 3.193 x 10-3 K-1; ln k = -2.36
50 °C (323.15 K): k = 0.1465 day-1; 1/T = 3.095 x 10-3 K-1; ln k = -1.92

Figure 2: Arrhenius plot of ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis, K-1), five points falling along a straight line of best fit with gradient -5.73 x 103 K and R2 = 0.99. Using the gradient, Ea = 5733 x 8.314 = 47.7 kJ mol-1. To estimate the uncertainty I drew the steepest and shallowest lines that passed through all of the error bars, giving gradients of about -6.5 x 103 K and -5.0 x 103 K, so Ea = 48 ± 6 kJ mol-1.

Conclusion

The data support my hypothesis. Ascorbic acid concentration fell steadily as storage temperature increased: after seven days the juice at 4 °C kept 94.7% of its initial vitamin C, while the juice at 50 °C kept only 35.9%. Because the error bars (± 3 to 4 mg dm-3) are tiny compared to the differences between temperatures (the smallest gap, between 20 and 30 °C, is 57 mg dm-3) these differences are not explained by measurement uncertainty alone. The linear fit (R2 = 0.98) shows a loss of about 5.7 mg dm-3 for every 1 °C, though the Arrhenius treatment is a better model since the percentage loss itself accelerates with temperature: k at 50 °C is 19 times larger than at 4 °C.

The Arrhenius plot was strongly linear (R2 = 0.99) and gave Ea = 48 ± 6 kJ mol-1. This lies in the range of roughly 40 to 60 kJ mol-1 that I found for ascorbic acid degradation in citrus juice (Burdurlu et al., 2006), so my result is consistent with the literature. Collision theory explains the trend: a higher temperature gives a larger fraction of molecules with energy of at least Ea, so the oxidation and hydrolysis steps happen faster. In addition, oxygen solubility falls with temperature, which should slow oxidation, so the fact that the overall rate still rises sharply shows the activation energy effect dominates in this range. I did not test this directly, so it is a reasoned suggestion only.

A limit on the conclusion is that I only measured one time point per temperature, so first-order kinetics is an assumption. If the loss were not first-order (for example, if it were fast at first and then slowed), the values of k and Ea would be only apparent values. The result that 4 °C seems to lie slightly off the line in Figure 2 may hint at this.

Evaluation

Strengths: using a standard solution made from a primary standard, a single batch of juice, foil-wrapped flasks, equal headspace, triplicate titrations with a rough titration first, and propagating uncertainty meant random error was small. The agreement of triplicate titres within 0.2 cm3 supports the precision.

Limitations and their effect:
1. Single storage time. With only the day 7 measurement, I could not check the order of reaction. Improvement: take samples after 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 days at each temperature and plot ln c against t; a straight line at each temperature would confirm first order, and the gradient would give k directly instead of an assumed value.
2. Oxidation by air in the flask. Each flask was opened to take 25.00 cm3 samples at the end, but I also lifted the lid at the start to check temperature, letting extra oxygen in. This probably increased loss slightly at all temperatures. Improvement: use sealed flasks with a septum, or a separate sealed vial for every time and temperature so each is opened only once.
3. End-point colour in dark samples. In the 50 °C juice the brown colour made the blue-black end point harder to see, which could shift the titre by about 0.1 to 0.2 cm3, a possible 2% effect at the lowest titre, larger than the ± 0.1 cm3 I assumed. Improvement: dilute the sample 1:1 with distilled water before titrating, or use a potentiometric end point with a platinum electrode.
4. Other reducing substances. Iodine can also react with other reducing compounds in juice (for example some polyphenols), so my values may overestimate true ascorbic acid, and the real fraction lost may differ. Improvement: compare the result with HPLC analysis if available, or run the titration on a pure ascorbic acid standard stored at the same temperatures to see how much of the change is due to ascorbic acid itself.
5. Temperature control. Water baths were checked once a day with a thermometer and varied by about ± 0.5 °C; the fridge fluctuated more. An error of 1 K at 4 °C changes k by about 7%, which could explain part of the deviation of the 4 °C point. Improvement: use a data logger in each environment.

Extension: repeating with a juice containing added preservatives, or with a sealed versus open container, would show how much oxygen rather than temperature is responsible for the loss.

Reference: Burdurlu, H.S., Koca, N. and Karadeniz, F. (2006) Degradation of vitamin C in citrus juice concentrates during storage. Journal of Food Engineering, 74, 211-216.

task: Chemistry internal assessment: investigate how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon.
text:
An investigation into how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of reaction with magnesium

Introduction and background

For my chemistry internal assessment I wanted to look at rates of reaction because we learned about collision theory in Topic 6 and I found it interesting that something so simple could be explained by particles hitting each other. Rates of reaction are important in industry, for example in the Haber process, where companies need the reaction to go fast enough to make money but they also have to be safe. Acids are also in everyday life, for example in stomach acid and in cleaning products, so I chose hydrochloric acid and magnesium because they are easy to get in the school lab and react quickly.

The equation for the reaction is:
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

Magnesium is a reactive metal in group 2 of the periodic table. It is above hydrogen in the reactivity series so it displaces hydrogen from acids. Magnesium is oxidised from 0 to +2 and hydrogen is reduced from +1 to 0, so this is a redox reaction. Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid so it completely dissociates in water into H+ and Cl- ions. The magnesium reacts with the H+ ions. The reaction is exothermic so some heat is released and the solution warms up. The rate of reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products are made. It can be measured by the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

Collision theory says that for a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and in the right orientation. If the concentration of acid is higher there are more H+ ions in the same volume so there are more frequent collisions per second between H+ ions and the magnesium surface. This means more successful collisions and a higher rate. So I predict that as concentration of acid increases the rate of reaction will increase. I also predict that the rate will double when the concentration doubles because there will be twice as many particles.

Research question: How does the concentration of hydrochloric acid (0.50, 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 mol dm-3) affect the rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon, measured by the time taken for the magnesium to disappear?

Variables

Independent variable: concentration of HCl (0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00 mol dm-3). I made these by diluting 2.00 mol dm-3 stock acid with distilled water using a measuring cylinder.
Dependent variable: time taken for the magnesium ribbon to fully react (disappear), measured in seconds with a stopwatch. The rate was calculated as 1/time.
Controlled variables: temperature (room temperature, about 22 °C), volume of acid (50.0 cm3), length of magnesium ribbon (2.0 cm), the same piece of ribbon from the same roll, and the same type of beaker (100 cm3).

Apparatus

Magnesium ribbon, ruler, scissors, sandpaper, 2.00 mol dm-3 hydrochloric acid, distilled water, 50 cm3 measuring cylinder (± 0.5 cm3), 100 cm3 beakers, stopwatch (± 0.01 s), thermometer, goggles.

Method

1. Put on goggles.
2. Cut 2.0 cm lengths of magnesium ribbon with scissors and clean them with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer.
3. Measure out the right amount of 2.00 mol dm-3 hydrochloric acid and distilled water in the measuring cylinder to make 50.0 cm3 of the required concentration, and pour into a beaker. For 0.50 mol dm-3 this was 12.5 cm3 acid and 37.5 cm3 water, for 1.00 it was 25 cm3 and 25 cm3, for 1.50 it was 37.5 cm3 and 12.5 cm3, and 2.00 was undiluted.
4. Drop the magnesium ribbon in and start the stopwatch at the same time.
5. Stop the stopwatch when the ribbon has completely disappeared.
6. Record the time.
7. Repeat for each concentration, doing each one twice.

Safety: hydrochloric acid at 2.00 mol dm-3 is corrosive so goggles were worn. Hydrogen is flammable so there were no flames near the experiment. Spills were wiped up straight away.

Raw data

Table 1: time for 2.0 cm of magnesium ribbon to react in 50.0 cm3 of acid
Concentration 0.50 mol dm-3: trial 1 142 s, trial 2 151 s
Concentration 1.00 mol dm-3: trial 1 71 s, trial 2 68 s
Concentration 1.50 mol dm-3: trial 1 49 s, trial 2 44 s
Concentration 2.00 mol dm-3: trial 1 36 s, trial 2 33 s

Observations: bubbles of gas formed on the surface of the magnesium and the ribbon floated up and down. The higher concentrations fizzed much more and the beaker felt warm at 2.00 mol dm-3.

The uncertainty of the stopwatch is ± 0.01 s and the measuring cylinder is ± 0.5 cm3. The uncertainty of the thermometer is ± 0.5 °C.

Processed data

I calculated the mean time and then the rate (1/t).

Concentration 0.50: mean time 146.5 s, rate = 1/146.5 = 0.0068 s-1
Concentration 1.00: mean time 69.5 s, rate = 1/69.5 = 0.0144 s-1
Concentration 1.50: mean time 46.5 s, rate = 1/46.5 = 0.0215 s-1
Concentration 2.00: mean time 34.5 s, rate = 1/34.5 = 0.0290 s-1

Figure 1: line graph of rate (s-1) against concentration of HCl (mol dm-3) with four points joined by a straight line of best fit that goes upwards from bottom left to top right and passes near the origin. The points are close to the line.

The graph shows that as the concentration gets higher the rate gets higher. It is a straight line so the rate is directly proportional to concentration. I worked out the gradient of the line which is about 0.0145 s-1 per mol dm-3. The values of rate divided by concentration are 0.0137, 0.0144, 0.0143 and 0.0145 which are almost the same, which shows it is proportional.

Conclusion

The results show that as the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases the rate of reaction increases. At 0.50 mol dm-3 the magnesium took 146.5 s to react but at 2.00 mol dm-3 it only took 34.5 s, so the reaction was about 4.2 times faster when the concentration was 4 times higher. The graph of rate against concentration was a straight line through nearly the origin so rate is directly proportional to concentration, which means the reaction is first order with respect to H+. This agrees with my hypothesis that doubling the concentration would double the rate: going from 0.50 to 1.00 the rate went from 0.0068 to 0.0144 which is 2.1 times bigger.

This can be explained by collision theory. At a higher concentration there are more H+ ions in the same volume so there are more collisions between H+ ions and the magnesium surface every second. More collisions means more successful collisions so the reaction is faster. The activation energy does not change because the temperature is the same.

So the hypothesis was supported by the data.

Evaluation

The investigation worked well because the results formed a straight line and the repeats were close to each other. However there were some problems that might have affected the results.

One problem was that the reaction is exothermic so the temperature of the acid went up during the reaction, especially in the 2.00 mol dm-3 acid. A higher temperature makes particles move faster so this would make the reaction faster than it should be at the higher concentrations. This could be improved by putting the beaker in a water bath to keep the temperature constant.

Another problem was that it was hard to tell exactly when the magnesium had completely disappeared, because the last bit of the ribbon was tiny and sometimes stuck to the side of the beaker. It also meant that the time for the 0.50 mol dm-3 acid had a range of 9 s between the repeats (142 and 151) which is bigger than the others. To improve this I could do more repeats, for example five instead of two, to get a better average.

The magnesium ribbon was cut by hand with scissors and a ruler so the lengths might not have been exactly 2.0 cm, and the ribbon might have been different thicknesses in places, so the surface area was probably not exactly the same each time. This would affect the rate because a bigger surface area means more collisions. To improve this I could use a balance to weigh the magnesium to the same mass, such as 0.050 g each time, instead of measuring the length.

There was also human error in starting and stopping the stopwatch because of reaction time. This could have made the times a little bit wrong. Using a data logger or gas syringe to measure the volume of hydrogen could be more accurate than judging by eye when the magnesium has disappeared.

I only used four concentrations so I could not be sure that the relationship stays a straight line for higher concentrations. In future I could test more concentrations such as 0.25, 0.75 and 2.50 mol dm-3. I could also investigate the effect of temperature or of surface area to see how they affect the rate of reaction, and compare the results to the effect of concentration.

Overall the investigation was successful in showing that rate increases with concentration and the method could be improved by controlling the temperature and measuring the mass of magnesium.

task: Chemistry internal assessment: investigate which brand of antacid tablet neutralises the most stomach acid.
text:
Which antacid is the best at neutralising acid?

Introduction

Many people get heartburn and take antacid tablets. I wanted to find out which antacid is the best so that people know what to buy. Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid and antacids are bases so they neutralise it. Antacids have different ingredients such as calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide and sodium hydrogencarbonate. The reaction of an acid and a base makes a salt and water, and with a carbonate it also makes carbon dioxide. I think that the most expensive antacid will be the best because it probably has more of the good ingredients in it.

Stomach acid is made in the stomach by cells in the stomach lining and it helps to break down food and kill bacteria that come in with the food. The stomach is very acidic, with a pH of about 2. Sometimes the acid goes up the oesophagus and this is what causes heartburn, which is painful. There are lots of adverts on TV for antacids and they all say that theirs works the fastest and the best, so I wanted to test this for myself and see if it is true. The pH scale goes from 0 to 14 and acids are below 7 and bases are above 7. Neutralisation is when the pH goes to 7. I looked at some websites and they said that calcium carbonate is the main ingredient in a lot of antacids but I did not write down which websites.

Research question: Which antacid tablet neutralises the most hydrochloric acid?

Hypothesis: Brand A will be best because it is the most expensive.

Variables

Independent variable: the brand of antacid tablet (Brand A, Brand B, Brand C).
Dependent variable: how much acid it neutralises.
Controlled variables: the amount of acid, the tablet, the temperature, the time.

Materials

3 types of antacid tablets, hydrochloric acid, sodium hydroxide, indicator, beaker, conical flask, burette, mortar and pestle, balance, water, safety goggles.

Method

1. Crush one tablet using the mortar and pestle.
2. Put the powder in a conical flask and add 50 cm3 of hydrochloric acid.
3. Leave it to react for a while until the fizzing has stopped.
4. Add a few drops of indicator.
5. Fill the burette with sodium hydroxide and titrate the leftover acid until the colour changes.
6. Record how much sodium hydroxide was needed.
7. Do it again with the other tablets.

Safety: wear goggles because the acid can hurt your eyes.

Results

Table of results (back titration)
Brand A: 24.2
Brand B: 31.5
Brand C: 18.9

I also did Brand A a second time and got a different number so I just used the first one. The tablets looked different, Brand B was bigger and Brand C was chalky and crumbly. All the tablets fizzed when the acid was added except for Brand B which only fizzed a little bit. The indicator went pink at the end point in each one.

Graph: bar chart of brand on the x-axis and the volume of sodium hydroxide on the y-axis. Brand B has the highest bar, then Brand A, then Brand C.

Analysis

The graph shows that Brand B has the highest bar and Brand C has the lowest. This means that Brand B had the most sodium hydroxide so it was the best at neutralising the acid. Brand A is in the middle and Brand C is the worst. The bars have different heights so the antacids are different from each other. Brand B is bigger than Brand A by about 7 and Brand C is lower than Brand A by about 5.

Conclusion

My hypothesis was not correct because Brand A was not the best antacid, Brand B was the best. So the most expensive antacid is not always the best one. Antacids work by neutralising stomach acid because they are bases so they react with the acid and make it less acidic, which makes the heartburn go away. Brand B probably has more calcium carbonate in it than the others which is why it is best. This shows that Brand B is the best antacid and people should buy Brand B if they have heartburn.

Evaluation

My experiment went quite well and I got results that showed which antacid was the best. However, there were some errors. The main source of error was human error, for example when I was reading the burette and judging the colour change, which could be a bit different every time, so my results may not be exact. Also I might have spilled some of the powder when I was crushing the tablets, which would change the result.

Another error was that the tablets are different sizes and weights so it is not a fair test. Also the time that I left the tablet in the acid was not the same each time because I got distracted. The reaction could have been not finished so the results are less accurate.

To improve the experiment I could be more careful and do it again with more brands, and use more accurate equipment. I could also do the experiment with a different acid. If I did it again I would also ask people which antacid they like the best to see if it agrees with my results.

I also think that the results could be wrong because the equipment might have been dirty from other people using it before me, and the burette might have had a leak. The sodium hydroxide might also have been the wrong concentration because I did not check the label properly. Another thing is that the teacher helped me with some of the steps so it might not be completely my own results. If I had more time I would have done more experiments and made a better table. It would also be good to find out how much each tablet costs so that people know which one is the best value for money, and then I could say which one people should buy.

Overall I am happy with my experiment and I think it was a success because I found out what I wanted to know.

task: Chemistry internal assessment: investigate how the enthalpy of combustion of the primary alcohols methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol changes with chain length, using a spirit burner and copper calorimeter.
text:
An investigation into the enthalpy of combustion of the alcohols

Introduction

Energy is one of the most important topics in modern chemistry and in everyday life. Humans have used the combustion of fuels for thousands of years, first with wood and later with coal, oil and gas. Today most of the world's energy still comes from burning fossil fuels, which has led to the release of large amounts of carbon dioxide and contributed to global warming. Because of this, scientists are looking for alternative fuels such as biofuels. Ethanol, which can be made by the fermentation of sugars from crops such as sugar cane and corn, is already blended into petrol in many countries. In Brazil many cars run on ethanol. This makes the alcohols an interesting family of compounds to study. I chose this topic because I am interested in sustainable energy and want to study chemical engineering at university.

Background theory

Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. The enthalpy change of a reaction, written as delta H, is the heat energy given out or taken in during a reaction at constant pressure. When the products have less enthalpy than the reactants, energy is released to the surroundings and delta H is negative. This is called an exothermic reaction. Combustion reactions are always exothermic. The standard enthalpy change of combustion, delta H c with a standard symbol, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, which are 298 K and 100 kPa, with all substances in their standard states.

The alcohols are an homologous series of organic compounds that contain the hydroxyl functional group, -OH. They have the general formula CnH2n+1OH. Methanol (CH3OH) has one carbon, ethanol (C2H5OH) has two, propan-1-ol (C3H7OH) has three and butan-1-ol (C4H9OH) has four. Members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties because they have the same functional group but their physical properties change gradually as the chain gets longer, for example the boiling point gets higher because there are stronger London dispersion forces between longer molecules. The alcohols also have hydrogen bonds between the -OH groups, which explains why they have higher boiling points than alkanes of a similar size.

The complete combustion of an alcohol produces carbon dioxide and water:
CH3OH + 1.5O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O
C3H7OH + 4.5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O
C4H9OH + 6O2 -> 4CO2 + 5H2O
If there is not enough oxygen the combustion is incomplete and carbon monoxide and carbon (soot) can be made instead, which gives a yellow smoky flame and less energy.

The enthalpy change of a reaction can be understood in terms of bond enthalpies. Energy is needed to break bonds in the reactants (endothermic) and energy is released when new bonds are made in the products (exothermic). The overall enthalpy change is the energy taken in to break bonds minus the energy given out when bonds are made. In a combustion, the bonds broken are C-H, C-C, C-O, O-H and O=O, while the bonds made are C=O in carbon dioxide and O-H in water. Bond enthalpy values from the data booklet are: C-H 414 kJ mol-1, C-C 346, C-O 358, O-H 463, O=O 498, C=O 804 (in carbon dioxide). Bond enthalpies are average values so calculations using them are only approximate and differ from experimental ones. A more accurate method is to use Hess's law, which says that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken. Using Hess's law, delta H of combustion can be found from standard enthalpies of formation: delta H = sum of delta H f of the products minus the sum of delta H f of the reactants.

As the number of carbon atoms in the alcohol increases, each extra CH2 group adds one more C-C bond and two more C-H bonds to be broken, and one more carbon dioxide and one more water to be formed. Therefore I would expect the enthalpy of combustion to become more exothermic by a roughly constant amount for each extra CH2, which is about 650 to 700 kJ mol-1 per CH2 group. The data booklet values for delta H of combustion are: methanol -726, ethanol -1367, propan-1-ol -2021 and butan-1-ol -2676 kJ mol-1.

The history of fuels shows how important energy is to society. Wood was the first fuel, and then charcoal, which burns hotter, was used to smelt metals. During the Industrial Revolution in Britain, coal powered steam engines in factories, trains and ships, and cities grew rapidly around coalfields. In the twentieth century oil became the most important fuel because it is a liquid that can be transported easily and has a high energy density, and it is refined by fractional distillation into petrol, diesel, kerosene and other products. Natural gas, mostly methane, is used for heating and electricity. All of these fossil fuels contain carbon that was stored in plants and animals millions of years ago, and when they are burned the carbon is released as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, which strengthens the greenhouse effect because carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has risen from about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 ppm today, and average global temperatures have risen by about 1.1 °C. This has led to melting ice caps, rising sea levels and more extreme weather, which is why governments signed agreements such as the Paris Agreement in 2015 to limit warming to well below 2 °C.

Because of this, the choice of fuel is an important decision. A good fuel should have a high enthalpy of combustion per gram or per mole, be easy to store and transport, burn cleanly without making a lot of smoke or poisonous gases, be affordable and be renewable if possible. Specific energy, the energy released per gram, is a more useful measure for vehicles than the energy per mole because the mass of the fuel that has to be carried matters. For example, the energy density of petrol is about 46 kJ g-1, of ethanol 30 kJ g-1 and of methanol 22 kJ g-1, which is why a car needs a larger volume of ethanol to travel the same distance as with petrol. Hydrogen has a very high specific energy of 142 kJ g-1 but it is difficult to store as it is a gas with a very low density. Alcohols are partially oxidised hydrocarbons because they already contain an oxygen atom, so they release less energy per gram than the equivalent alkane, but they burn more cleanly.

The cleaner combustion of alcohols also matters for air quality. Burning petrol in car engines can produce carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides and particulates, which cause smog and respiratory problems in cities. Adding ethanol to petrol (for example E10, which is 10% ethanol) increases the oxygen content of the fuel and helps it to burn more completely. However, growing crops for biofuel takes land that could be used to grow food and can cause deforestation, so there is an ethical debate about food versus fuel. Second-generation biofuels made from waste materials such as straw and wood chips are being developed to try to avoid this problem.

It is also useful to define some other terms. The enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. The specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 K, and for water it is 4.18 J g-1 K-1, which is quite high because of hydrogen bonding between the water molecules. This is why water is used as the liquid in calorimetry experiments: it absorbs a lot of heat for each degree rise in temperature. The limitations of calorimetry include the heat transfer to the surroundings, the incomplete combustion, evaporation of the fuel from the wick, and the fact that the conditions of the experiment are not standard conditions. In a bomb calorimeter, the fuel is burned in excess oxygen at high pressure in a sealed steel container surrounded by water, so almost all of the heat is transferred, which makes it much more accurate.

Calorimetry is the experimental measurement of heat energy transferred. The heat energy gained by water can be found with the equation q = m c delta T, where m is the mass of water in grams, c is the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J g-1 K-1) and delta T is the temperature change. If the heat released by the burning fuel is assumed to be all transferred to the water, then the enthalpy of combustion can be found by dividing q by the number of moles of fuel burned. In real experiments much of the heat is lost to the surroundings, to heating the calorimeter and the air, so values are always less exothermic than the literature values.

Research question: How does the number of carbon atoms in the alcohol (methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol) affect the enthalpy of combustion, measured by heating water in a copper calorimeter with a spirit burner?

Hypothesis: the enthalpy of combustion will become more negative as the number of carbon atoms increases, because there are more bonds to break and more carbon dioxide and water molecules are formed.

Variables

Independent variable: the alcohol used (methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol).
Dependent variable: enthalpy of combustion in kJ mol-1, calculated from the temperature rise of the water and the mass of fuel burned.
Controlled variables: volume of water (100.0 cm3, assumed 100.0 g), the same copper calorimeter, distance between the flame and the bottom of the calorimeter (about 3 cm), starting temperature of the water (about 20 °C), use of a draught shield, same thermometer and same balance.

Method

1. Measure 100.0 cm3 of water in a measuring cylinder and pour it into the copper calorimeter, which is held on a clamp stand above a heat-proof mat.
2. Weigh a spirit burner containing methanol on a balance and record the mass.
3. Record the starting temperature of the water.
4. Light the wick and put the burner under the calorimeter. Stir the water gently with the thermometer.
5. When the temperature has risen by about 20 °C, put out the flame with the cap and record the highest temperature.
6. Reweigh the burner and record the new mass.
7. Repeat with ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol using fresh water each time.

The burners were all the same type of glass spirit burner with a cotton wick, and the calorimeter was a copper can with a capacity of 200 cm3 supported by a clamp. The wick was trimmed to the same length each time. A heat-proof mat protected the bench.

Safety: the alcohols are flammable and methanol is toxic, so the room was ventilated, goggles were worn, bottles of fuel were kept away from the flame, and long hair was tied back. The calorimeter was hot afterwards.

Results

Table of data (one run for each alcohol)
Methanol: mass burned 1.21 g, temperature rise 18.5 °C
Ethanol: mass burned 1.05 g, temperature rise 19.0 °C
Propan-1-ol: mass burned 0.98 g, temperature rise 20.5 °C
Butan-1-ol: mass burned 0.92 g, temperature rise 21.5 °C

Balance uncertainty ± 0.01 g, thermometer ± 0.5 °C.

Processing

Sample calculation for methanol:
q = m c delta T = 100.0 x 4.18 x 18.5 = 7733 J = 7.73 kJ
moles of methanol = 1.21 / 32.04 = 0.0378 mol
enthalpy of combustion = -7.73 / 0.0378 = -205 kJ mol-1

The other alcohols were calculated in the same way:
Ethanol: q = 7942 J, 0.0228 mol, enthalpy of combustion -349 kJ mol-1
Propan-1-ol: q = 8569 J, 0.0163 mol, enthalpy of combustion -526 kJ mol-1
Butan-1-ol: q = 8987 J, 0.0124 mol, enthalpy of combustion -724 kJ mol-1

Figure 1: bar chart of experimental enthalpy of combustion (kJ mol-1) for the four alcohols, with bars getting larger from methanol to butan-1-ol, and next to each bar a second bar for the literature value which is much taller.

Conclusion

The results show that the enthalpy of combustion becomes more exothermic as the number of carbon atoms increases, from -205 kJ mol-1 for methanol to -724 kJ mol-1 for butan-1-ol. This agrees with my hypothesis and with the literature values, which also increase with the length of the chain. This is because longer alcohols have more bonds to break and make more carbon dioxide and water. However my values were much smaller than the literature values, for example ethanol -349 compared with -1367 kJ mol-1.

Evaluation

The experimental values are much lower than the literature values because a lot of heat was lost to the surroundings and not all of it went into the water. Some heat also heated the copper calorimeter itself. The combustion might have been incomplete, with soot on the bottom of the calorimeter. To improve, a draught shield could be used and the experiment could be repeated more times. A bomb calorimeter would give more accurate results.

task: DP Biology extended response (Paper 2 style, 12 marks): Explain how antibiotic resistance can arise and spread in populations of bacteria, and discuss measures that could be used to limit it.
text:
Antibiotic resistance is an evolutionary process, and it can be explained by natural selection acting on variation that already exists in a bacterial population.

How resistance arises

Variation in a bacterial population begins with mutation. DNA replication in bacteria is very accurate but not perfect, and with populations of billions of cells, random mutations occur constantly. Mutations are random, and they arise before the antibiotic is applied; the antibiotic does not cause them. Occasionally a mutation changes a gene so that the cell is less affected by an antibiotic. For example, a mutation in the gene for a penicillin-binding protein can alter the shape of the enzyme so penicillin can no longer bind to it, or a mutation may change a ribosomal subunit so that tetracycline cannot attach. Other resistant bacteria produce beta-lactamase, which breaks down the beta-lactam ring of penicillin.

When the antibiotic is present it acts as a selection pressure. Susceptible bacteria cannot make a functional cell wall (in the case of penicillin) and are killed or stop growing, whereas the rare resistant bacteria survive. Those survivors reproduce by binary fission, and as bacteria can divide as often as every 20 minutes, a single resistant cell can become a large resistant population within a day. The allele for resistance is therefore passed on to offspring and its frequency in the population increases over generations. This is natural selection: variation, a selective pressure, differential survival and reproduction, and inheritance. It is important to note that individual bacteria do not become resistant by "getting used to" the drug; the population changes, not the individual.

How resistance spreads

Spread within a species happens by vertical transmission, from parent cell to daughter cells, as described above. However, bacteria can also share genes by horizontal gene transfer, which is how resistance spreads so quickly between different cells and even different species. In conjugation, a plasmid carrying a resistance gene is copied and passed from one bacterium to another through a pilus. Many plasmids carry several resistance genes at once, so a single transfer can make a bacterium resistant to multiple antibiotics, and this explains multidrug-resistant strains such as MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus). In hospitals, antibiotics are used heavily, so selection is strong, and patients with weakened immune systems are easily infected; resistant bacteria are carried on hands, equipment and surfaces.

Measures to limit resistance

1. Reduce unnecessary use. Antibiotics have no effect on viral infections such as colds and influenza, so prescribing them for viral illness only imposes selection pressure with no benefit. Doctors can prescribe only when a bacterial infection is confirmed, ideally after testing which antibiotic the strain is susceptible to. This is effective in principle, but it is hard to enforce because patients expect treatment and in some countries antibiotics are sold without a prescription.

2. Complete the course. Patients who stop treatment as soon as they feel better may leave behind the partly resistant bacteria, which can then multiply. Completing the course kills more of the population including those with weak resistance. Some recent evidence suggests shorter, evidence-based courses may be adequate, so this advice is under review.

3. Limit agricultural use. In many countries large quantities of antibiotics are given to healthy livestock to promote growth. This exposes bacteria to low doses, which favours the selection of resistance, and resistant bacteria can pass to humans through meat or the environment. Banning growth promotion, as the EU did in 2006, reduces this selection pressure. Resistance does not vanish immediately because plasmid genes can persist.

4. Infection control. Handwashing, isolating patients with resistant infections and cleaning equipment prevent spread without using any antibiotics at all, so they remove selection pressure completely.

5. Developing new drugs and using combinations. Using two antibiotics with different mechanisms means a bacterium would need two independent resistance mutations at once, which is very unlikely. New antibiotics are costly to develop and have low profit for companies, so progress is slow, and any new drug will also eventually face resistance.

Evaluation

No single measure is enough. Reducing use and infection control address the cause (selection pressure and transmission), whereas new drugs only treat the consequence. Because resistance spreads across borders, measures must be international to be effective; one country limiting use does not help if resistant strains arrive from elsewhere. Moreover, resistance genes may persist even when the antibiotic is withdrawn if they do not carry a large fitness cost to bacteria, so reversal is slow. Therefore a combination of stewardship, hygiene and research, supported by international policy, offers the most realistic way to slow resistance, though not to stop it completely, because natural selection will always favour resistant bacteria whenever antibiotics are used.

task: DP Biology extended response (Paper 2 style, 12 marks): Explain how antibiotic resistance can arise and spread in populations of bacteria, and discuss measures that could be used to limit it.
text:
Antibiotic resistance is when bacteria become resistant to antibiotics so that the antibiotics no longer kill them. This is a big problem in the world today because it means that infections which used to be easy to treat are now very hard to treat and people can die from them.

How it arises

Resistance arises because of natural selection. In a population of bacteria there is variation, which means that some bacteria are different from each other. This is caused by mutations in the DNA. Some bacteria may have a mutation which makes them resistant to an antibiotic. When someone takes an antibiotic, it kills most of the bacteria, but the resistant bacteria survive because they are not affected by the antibiotic. The survivors then reproduce and pass on the resistance gene to their offspring. After many generations the whole population is resistant. This is called survival of the fittest. Bacteria reproduce very quickly, so this can happen in a short time.

Sometimes the bacteria mutate because they are exposed to the antibiotic so they adapt to it and become resistant. They can also get resistance from other bacteria because they can pass on plasmids which have resistance genes on them. A plasmid is a small circle of DNA. This is called conjugation. So bacteria that were not resistant can become resistant by getting a plasmid from another bacterium.

How it spreads

Resistant bacteria can spread from person to person by coughing, touching surfaces and in hospitals. In hospitals many people are ill and take antibiotics so there are lots of resistant bacteria there, such as MRSA. People who travel can spread resistant bacteria to other countries. The bacteria can also spread through food and water. Farmers give antibiotics to animals, and the resistant bacteria can spread to people who eat the meat.

Also the more antibiotics are used the faster the bacteria become resistant, because there are more bacteria being exposed to them. Antibiotics are often prescribed by doctors when they are not needed, for example for viruses like the flu or a cold. Antibiotics do not work on viruses and this makes the bacteria in the body more resistant, so it is overuse.

Measures to limit resistance

There are some things that could be done to stop antibiotic resistance from getting worse.

Firstly, doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when they are really needed, so not for viral infections. This means fewer bacteria are exposed to antibiotics, so there is less selection for resistance. Patients should not ask for antibiotics for minor illnesses.

Secondly, patients should always finish the full course of antibiotics, even if they feel better, so that all the bacteria are killed and none are left to become resistant. If they stop early, the strongest bacteria will survive and multiply.

Thirdly, hospitals should have good hygiene such as washing hands and cleaning equipment, so that resistant bacteria cannot spread from patient to patient. Patients with MRSA can be isolated.

Fourthly, farmers should not use antibiotics on healthy animals, so that there are fewer resistant bacteria in food. In the EU antibiotics are no longer allowed to be used for growth promotion.

Finally, scientists should develop new antibiotics to replace the ones that no longer work. They could also use more than one antibiotic at the same time.

Evaluation

Some of these measures are better than others. Stopping unnecessary prescriptions is probably the best because it reduces the cause of the problem. Finishing the course of antibiotics is good but not always followed by patients because they forget or feel better. New antibiotics are expensive to make, and companies do not make much money from them, so not many are being developed. Overall I think that a combination of all of these measures would be the best way to reduce antibiotic resistance, but it will be difficult because it needs everybody to cooperate.

In conclusion, antibiotic resistance happens through natural selection and the spread of plasmids, and it can be limited by using antibiotics less and by good hygiene. It is an important global issue which affects everyone and so governments and individuals must work together to solve it.
