task: DP Economics internal assessment commentary (maximum 800 words) on a published news article from the last 12 months, using a key concept from the syllabus: 'Cocoa prices hit record high as poor West African harvests squeeze chocolate makers' (Reuters, 12 April 2024).
text:
Commentary 1
Article: 'Cocoa prices hit record high as poor West African harvests squeeze chocolate makers', Reuters, 12 April 2024
Unit: Microeconomics (competitive markets, elasticities)
Key concept: Interdependence
Word count: 745

The article reports that the world cocoa price has risen from about $4,000 to over $10,000 per tonne in a year, because heavy rain and disease cut harvests in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, which grow around 60% of the world's cocoa. Chocolate makers say they will raise prices or shrink bars, and the Ivorian government has raised the guaranteed farmgate price.

Diagram 1: the world market for cocoa. Price per tonne ($) on the vertical axis, quantity (tonnes) on the horizontal axis. A steep demand curve D, labelled price inelastic. Supply S1 shifts left to S2. Equilibrium moves from A (P1 = $4,000, Q1) to B (P2 = $10,000, Q2), with Q2 only slightly below Q1.

Disease and flooding raise production costs and reduce the quantity farmers can supply at every price, so supply decreases from S1 to S2. At P1 there is excess demand, so buyers bid the price up, causing a contraction in quantity demanded along D and an extension of quantity supplied along S2 until the market clears at B. Because demand is price inelastic, price rises 150% while quantity traded falls only a little. Demand is inelastic because cocoa is a necessary input, cocoa butter has no real substitute in chocolate, and cocoa is a small share of a bar's cost, so buyers cut back slowly. I estimate PED of roughly -0.3.

Revenue shows how gains are unequal. With inelastic demand, a farmer with a normal harvest earns more because P2 x Q2 is much larger than P1 x Q1. A farmer whose crop failed sells less and may earn less despite the higher price.

This illustrates interdependence. The cocoa market links West African farmers, traders, firms such as Mars and Lindt, consumers in Europe and the USA, and governments. A weather event in one region changes firms' costs on another continent.

Diagram 2: the market for chocolate bars in the UK. Price per bar (£) against quantity. Supply S1 shifts left to S2 because cocoa, a factor input, costs more. Demand D is flatter than in Diagram 1, labelled relatively elastic. Price rises from P1 to P2 by a smaller percentage, and quantity falls from Q1 to Q2 by a larger percentage, than in Diagram 1.

Because consumers can switch to biscuits and sweets, demand for chocolate is more elastic than demand for cocoa, so firms can pass on only part of the cost. This explains shrinkflation, a hidden price rise per gram. The rest of the burden falls on firms as lower margins; the more inelastic party bears more. If chocolate PED is about -1.2, a 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by roughly 12%, so a firm that passed on the full cost increase would lose revenue. This is why large firms also hedge by buying cocoa on futures contracts, which links them to financial markets and delays the effect on shelf prices by several months.

Evaluation

In the short run the effect is likely as shown, but in the long run supply of cocoa is more elastic. Farmers can plant resistant trees, though these take three to five years to bear pods, and the high price gives countries such as Ecuador an incentive to expand output, shifting supply right and lowering price. Record prices may also push firms to develop substitutes, making demand more elastic. The record price may therefore not last.

Stakeholders are affected unequally. The Ivorian government's higher farmgate price is a price floor that protects farmers when prices fall, but when world prices spike, farmers still receive only a fraction of the market price, so much of the gain goes to traders. Low-income households may be hurt more by dearer chocolate, but because it is not a necessity the equity impact is probably small. The article gives no data on cocoa's share of final price or on elasticity, so my judgement that firms pass on only part of the cost is a reasoned assumption, and shop price data over the next year would test it.

Overall, interdependence means the shock reaches everyone, but unevenly: farmers with failed crops lose, while traders and surviving growers may gain.

task: DP Economics internal assessment commentary (maximum 800 words) on a published news article from the last 12 months, using a key concept from the syllabus: 'Cocoa prices hit record high as poor West African harvests squeeze chocolate makers' (Reuters, 12 April 2024).
text:
Commentary 1
Article: Cocoa prices hit record high as poor West African harvests squeeze chocolate makers, Reuters
Key concept: Scarcity
Word count: 795

Cocoa prices have reached a record high because there have been bad harvests in West Africa. Heavy rain and disease have damaged the cocoa trees in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire. Chocolate makers are worried about the high prices and say they will have to put up the price of chocolate and make the bars smaller. This is an example of the key concept of scarcity because there is not enough cocoa for everyone who wants it, and so the price goes up.

Diagram 1: supply and demand diagram for cocoa. Price on the y-axis and quantity on the x-axis. The supply curve S moves to the left to S1 and the price goes up from P to P1. The demand curve D is the same. The quantity goes down from Q to Q1. The axes are labelled but the diagram does not show the equilibrium points with letters.

As we can see on the diagram, the supply of cocoa has decreased because of the poor harvests. This means that supply shifts to the left. When the supply decreases, the price goes up because there is a shortage of cocoa. This is the law of supply and demand. The price of cocoa goes from P to P1 and the quantity goes from Q to Q1. The demand for cocoa is inelastic because chocolate makers need cocoa to make chocolate so they will always buy it, even if the price rises. Therefore the price rises a lot.

The article says that the price of cocoa is now over $10,000 per tonne, which is more than double what it was last year. This is a big increase and it will affect a lot of different people. The farmers are affected because many of their crops have been damaged and so they will earn less money. The chocolate makers are affected because they will have to pay more for cocoa, so their costs go up. Consumers are affected because chocolate will cost more. The government is affected too because they might get less tax from the farmers.

Diagram 2: chocolate market diagram with the supply curve shifting to the left because costs go up, with the price of chocolate rising. The diagram has price and quantity on the axes and a curve labelled S1 shifting to S2.

The second diagram shows that the cost of making chocolate has gone up so the supply of chocolate decreases. This means that the price of chocolate will go up and fewer people will buy chocolate. Companies like Hershey's and Cadbury will have to increase prices. Some companies have already said that they will reduce the size of the bars instead of putting up the price, which is called shrinkflation, so that people do not notice. This is a good way for a company to keep its profits the same without upsetting people.

The key concept of scarcity applies because the resources, in this case cocoa beans, are scarce and so people must make choices about what to do with them. Firms must choose whether to put up their prices or reduce the size of the bars, and consumers must choose whether to buy chocolate or something else. This is the basic economic problem of scarcity and choice, which is what economics is all about. Scarcity also means that resources have an opportunity cost: if farmers grow cocoa they cannot grow other crops. So there is a trade-off.

There are some other things to consider. The price of cocoa might come down in the future because the farmers will grow more cocoa when the prices are high and then supply will increase again. This will shift the supply curve to the right and the price will go back down. On the other hand, climate change might mean that the bad weather in West Africa continues, so the price might stay high. It is difficult to know what will happen. The government of Côte d'Ivoire has also raised the price it pays farmers, which is good for the farmers.

In conclusion the high cocoa prices will have negative effects on chocolate makers and consumers and some farmers. Chocolate makers will probably pass the higher costs onto consumers by raising prices or using shrinkflation, and some people will buy less chocolate. However some farmers who have good harvests will make more money. Overall the poor harvests and the higher price show the importance of the concept of scarcity in economics.

task: DP Geography fieldwork report: investigate how channel characteristics and bedload change downstream along a upland river, in line with the Bradshaw model.
text:
How do channel characteristics and bedload change downstream along the River Esk, North Yorkshire?

1. Fieldwork question and geographic context

Fieldwork question: To what extent do channel width, depth, velocity, discharge and bedload size change with distance downstream along the upper 8 km of the River Esk, and do these changes follow the Bradshaw model?

This question comes from the syllabus topic of freshwater: drainage basins and the changes that occur along a river's long profile. Bradshaw (1978) proposed that, as distance from the source increases, channel width, depth, discharge, velocity and load quantity increase, whereas the size of the bedload and the channel roughness decrease. The question is geographic because it relates to spatial patterns, scale, and to physical processes (erosion, transport and deposition) that explain them.

The River Esk rises on the moorland of the North York Moors at about 420 m above sea level and flows east towards Whitby. I studied the 8 km stretch between its upland source area (grid reference NZ 7011, Site 1) and a point near the village of Castleton (Site 8). Land use changes from heather moorland at Site 1 to pasture and small areas of woodland near Site 8. The geology is mostly sandstone and shale, which are hard enough to produce angular stones in the upper reaches, and the catchment area above Site 8 is roughly 40 km2. Climate is wetter in the uplands (about 1000 mm of rain per year) so the upper catchment has frequent runoff and steep channels. Fieldwork took place on 14 and 15 March after a dry week, so flow was moderate and safe.

Hypotheses:
H1: Velocity, width, depth and discharge will increase downstream.
H2: Bedload size (long axis) will decrease downstream.
The null hypothesis is that there is no relationship between distance downstream and each variable.

2. Methods of investigation

I chose eight sites at 1 km intervals using systematic sampling to give a regular spread of data along the 8 km stretch, which is suitable for studying a continuous gradient; the sites were chosen on straight stretches without bridges or tributaries entering immediately upstream, so that channel conditions were not distorted by obvious human structures. Distance downstream was measured from a map using a string along the channel (scale 1:25,000) and checked using the GPS on my phone (± 5 m).

At each site I measured:
- Channel width: a tape measure across the water surface from bank to bank (± 0.05 m), taken once at a representative cross-section because the channel was uniform within 10 m.
- Depth: a metre ruler placed at 10 equal intervals across the channel (every 10% of the width), because river beds are irregular and a single depth would be unrepresentative. Mean depth was calculated (± 0.01 m).
- Velocity: a hydroprop flow meter at 0.6 of the depth, measured three times and averaged, which was chosen because the flow at 0.6 depth is close to the mean velocity of the water column, and flow meter is more accurate than the orange float method. Timing the float would have given a surface velocity, which is faster than the mean velocity and depends on the wind.
- Bedload: the long (a) axis of 10 stones, selected at random by walking across the channel and picking up the stone at the toe each step, without looking down, to avoid selecting the most attractive stone (bias). A sample of 10 is small, but time was limited (we had one day); I accepted this limit. Measured with a ruler (± 1 mm).

Risk assessment: wet, slippery rocks, cold water and floods were possible hazards. We worked in groups of three, wore wellingtons and buoyancy aids at deeper sites, checked the Environment Agency river level beforehand and did not enter water deeper than knee height.

3. Quality and treatment of information collected

Table 1: raw data and calculated values

Site (distance from source, km) / width (m) / mean depth (m) / mean velocity (m/s) / cross-sectional area (m2) / discharge (m3/s)
Site 1 (1 km): 1.4 / 0.12 / 0.18 / 0.17 / 0.03
Site 2 (2 km): 2.1 / 0.15 / 0.24 / 0.32 / 0.08
Site 3 (3 km): 2.9 / 0.19 / 0.31 / 0.55 / 0.17
Site 4 (4 km): 3.6 / 0.22 / 0.29 / 0.79 / 0.23
Site 5 (5 km): 4.4 / 0.26 / 0.42 / 1.14 / 0.48
Site 6 (6 km): 5.6 / 0.31 / 0.47 / 1.74 / 0.82
Site 7 (7 km): 6.1 / 0.30 / 0.55 / 1.83 / 1.01
Site 8 (8 km): 7.3 / 0.36 / 0.58 / 2.63 / 1.52

Cross-sectional area = width x mean depth, and discharge = cross-sectional area x mean velocity. The values are given to two significant figures where the depth was measured to the nearest centimetre.

Table 2: median bedload long axis (n = 10 per site), mm
Site 1: 112; Site 2: 96; Site 3: 98; Site 4: 74; Site 5: 63; Site 6: 51; Site 7: 52; Site 8: 38.
The interquartile range at Site 1 was 40 mm and at Site 8 it was 16 mm, which shows that stones were more varied in the upper reaches.

Presentation: Figure 1 is a map of the River Esk at 1:25,000 with the eight sites marked by numbered dots, a north arrow, and a scale bar. Figure 2 is a line graph of mean width, depth and velocity against distance downstream, with width on the primary axis (m) and velocity on a secondary axis (m/s), showing rising lines for each. Figure 3 is a scatter graph of discharge against distance with an upward curve (exponential rather than linear). Figure 4 is a scatter graph of bedload median long axis (mm) against distance with a downward line of best fit. Figure 5 is a long section proportional-circle-style diagram: cross-sectional channel profiles drawn to scale for Sites 1, 4 and 8, which makes the deepening and widening obvious.

Statistical treatment: I used Spearman's rank correlation for distance against velocity and distance against bedload size because the data are ordinal-scalable, n is small (8), and the relationships might not be perfectly linear.
Velocity: sum of d2 = 2, so rs = 1 - (6 x 2) / (8 x (64 - 1)) = 1 - 12/504 = +0.98.
Bedload size: sum of d2 = 164, so rs = 1 - (6 x 164) / 504 = 1 - 1.95 = -0.95.
For n = 8 the critical value at the 5% significance level (two-tailed) is 0.74 and at the 1% level it is 0.88. Both coefficients exceed 0.88, so I can reject the null hypothesis at the 99% confidence level.

4. Written analysis

Channel dimensions. Width increased steadily from 1.4 m at Site 1 to 7.3 m at Site 8, a 5.2-fold increase, while the mean depth increased from 0.12 m to 0.36 m (3-fold). Therefore width increased proportionally more than depth; the width-to-depth ratio rose from 11.7 at Site 1 to 20.3 at Site 8, meaning the channel became relatively broader and flatter. This pattern is consistent with the greater lateral than vertical erosion typical of a river as the valley widens and tributaries add water. The fall in depth between Site 6 and Site 7 (0.31 to 0.30 m) is an anomaly: Site 7 was in a wider pool with a gravel bar on one bank, so depth was measured in a section where flow had spread out.

Velocity. Mean velocity increased from 0.18 m/s at Site 1 to 0.58 m/s at Site 8 (rs = +0.98, significant at 99%). This is the opposite of what many students expect, because upstream channels are steeper, but the bed there is rough with large boulders (112 mm median stones) and shallow flow, so friction with the bed is large compared with the amount of water. Downstream, the hydraulic radius increases (the ratio of cross-section area to wetted perimeter), so a smaller proportion of the water is in contact with the bed and friction falls, so the water moves faster. One anomaly is Site 4, with a velocity (0.29 m/s) lower than Site 3 (0.31). On my map I could see that Site 4 is immediately upstream of a meander bend and there was a small weir, which slowed the flow by backing water up.

Discharge. Discharge increased from 0.03 to 1.52 m3/s, a 50-fold increase. Most of this increase comes from the product of the three variables that all increase: area increased 15-fold and velocity 3-fold. The graph of discharge against distance is an upward curve and not a straight line, so that discharge increases at an increasing rate. This follows because discharge is a product of three variables. Also the catchment area adds more tributaries and groundwater between the sites, particularly between Sites 5 and 6 where I noted two tributary streams entering (discharge doubled, 0.48 to 0.82 m3/s), compared with a change from 0.17 to 0.23 between Sites 3 and 4. This supports the idea that discharge rises because of the greater drainage area.

Bedload. The median long axis of stones decreased from 112 mm to 38 mm (rs = -0.95, significant at 99%). The explanation is attrition (stones collide with each other and the bed so they become smaller and rounder) and abrasion, together with selective deposition: as velocity rises, the river has more energy to transport smaller particles but the largest ones are left behind where they cannot be moved. I also recorded the shape of the stones using a Power's roundness index in the field, finding that Site 1 stones were angular (index 1 to 2) and Site 8 stones were sub-rounded (index 3 to 4). The two anomalies are Site 3 (98 mm, larger than Site 2) and Site 7 (52 mm, larger than Site 6). At Site 3 there was a steep slope and a landslip on the bank adding new, coarse, angular rock to the channel, and at Site 7 a small tributary may have delivered sediment from hillslope; both show that local influences affect the pattern.

Overall, the pattern fits the Bradshaw model: width, depth, velocity and discharge increased, while bedload size decreased.

5. Conclusion

The data show that the River Esk follows the Bradshaw model of downstream changes: width increased 5.2 times, depth 3 times, velocity 3.2 times and discharge about 50 times over 8 km, and median bedload size decreased from 112 to 38 mm. The strong Spearman coefficients (+0.98 and -0.95) are significant at the 1% level so the hypotheses are supported and the null hypotheses can be rejected. However, the model is general; the data also show that local factors such as tributaries, a weir and a landslip created anomalies at Sites 3, 4 and 7.

6. Evaluation

Reliability and limitations: (1) The sample of ten stones per site is small, and the Site 3 and 7 anomalies could be caused by sampling variation. A sample of 30 stones would give a more reliable median, and standard deviation or confidence intervals could then be calculated. (2) Velocity was measured only at three points at 0.6 depth in the centre of the channel, so the average velocity might be overestimated, since banks are slower. Taking measurements at 3 points across the channel would give a better average. (3) Fieldwork took place on just two days after a dry week, so the results represent low-to-moderate flow only; in a flood, the velocity and discharge would be different, and I cannot generalise to other seasons. Repeating in autumn would show whether the pattern holds. (4) The eight sites on only one river make it difficult to conclude that all rivers follow the model, and with n = 8 critical values are high. Using a comparison river (such as the River Rye) would add confidence. (5) Measuring width and depth to a certain level of accuracy relied on judging where the water edge was, which could be ± 5 cm at the shallow sites, a bigger percentage error at Site 1 (3.5% of width) than at Site 8.

Strengths were the systematic sampling design, the use of a flow meter instead of floats, random selection of stones and the statistical tests.

Bibliography
Bradshaw, M. (1978) The Earth's Changing Surface. London: Hodder & Stoughton.
Ordnance Survey (2019) OS Explorer OL27 North York Moors Eastern area, 1:25,000.
Environment Agency (2024) River levels and flood data, accessed 13 March.
Power's roundness scale, from field guide provided by teacher.

task: DP Geography fieldwork report: investigate how environmental quality changes with distance from the central business district in an urban area.
text:
Does environmental quality improve with distance from the CBD in Nottingham?

Introduction

My fieldwork was about urban environmental quality in Nottingham, which is a city in the East Midlands of England. Nottingham has a population of about 330,000 people and was once an important centre for lace making and the Raleigh bicycle company. Like most cities in the UK, it has a central business district (CBD) with lots of shops, offices, and busy roads, and then residential suburbs further out. We learned in class that the Burgess concentric zone model says that land use and the quality of the environment changes as you move away from the CBD, with the poorer housing near the centre and better housing in the suburbs. I wanted to find out if this is true in Nottingham.

My fieldwork question is: Does the environmental quality improve with distance from the CBD in Nottingham?

My hypothesis is that environmental quality will get better the further away from the CBD you are, because there will be less traffic and noise and more green space. The null hypothesis is that there is no relationship between environmental quality and distance from the CBD.

Nottingham is in the East Midlands and the River Trent goes through the south of the city. The route I chose went along Mansfield Road, which is a main road going north out of the city centre from the Old Market Square. The area to the north of the centre has mixed land uses and the neighbourhoods include Sherwood and Arnold, which are mainly residential.

Methods

On the 12th of October we went to Nottingham on a school trip and collected data at ten sites on a transect along Mansfield Road from the city centre to the suburb of Arnold. I chose a transect because it is a good way of seeing how something changes along a line. The sites were about 400 m apart, but because we ran out of time Sites 9 and 10 were further apart (about 700 m). At each site we carried out an environmental quality survey (EQS). This is a table where you score different things from -2 (bad) to +2 (good), such as the amount of litter, graffiti, noise, traffic, condition of buildings, and amount of greenery. We added up the scores to get a total out of 30 for each site, after adjusting the scale to be positive. In my group there were four people and each did the survey separately, then we averaged the scores. I also counted the traffic for 5 minutes at each site and measured the noise with a decibel meter app on my phone. Distance from the CBD was measured using Google Maps.

I chose the EQS because it is the standard method used for this kind of fieldwork and it is quick, and because it uses lots of criteria so it is a more balanced picture of environmental quality. I chose a transect because it follows the model's idea of getting further from the centre.

Before going out I looked at maps of the city to plan my route and worked out where the sites would be. I decided to use Mansfield Road because it is straight, runs directly out of the centre and has buses, so it was easy to get to. I thought this was better than a random sample because with a random sample the sites might not be in a line. We also tested the survey sheet at one site first to make sure everybody understood how to score each category, and we agreed that a score of -2 would be for things like heaps of rubbish or boarded-up buildings, and +2 for things like clean pavements and well kept gardens. Data collection took about four hours in total, starting at 9:30 am. The traffic was counted by standing at the side of the road and counting each car, bus, van and lorry that went past in either direction, and bicycles were not included. The noise was measured by holding the phone at about chest height facing the road for one minute and writing down the average reading.

Risk assessment: we had to be careful when crossing roads and stay together in groups. Teachers were nearby. We wore bright clothing and did not go anywhere dangerous.

Results

Table 1: results at each site
Site 1, 0.1 km from CBD: EQS score 8, traffic count 112 vehicles, noise 78 dB
Site 2, 0.5 km: EQS 10, traffic 104, noise 75 dB
Site 3, 0.9 km: EQS 9, traffic 98, noise 76 dB
Site 4, 1.3 km: EQS 14, traffic 85, noise 71 dB
Site 5, 1.7 km: EQS 17, traffic 67, noise 69 dB
Site 6, 2.1 km: EQS 15, traffic 70, noise 68 dB
Site 7, 2.5 km: EQS 21, traffic 55, noise 64 dB
Site 8, 2.9 km: EQS 19, traffic 58, noise 63 dB
Site 9, 3.6 km: EQS 24, traffic 41, noise 59 dB
Site 10, 4.3 km: EQS 26, traffic 33, noise 57 dB

I presented the results as a scatter graph. Figure 1: scatter graph of EQS score on the y-axis against distance from the CBD on the x-axis with a line of best fit sloping upwards from bottom left to top right. Figure 2: bar chart of traffic count at each site showing the bars getting shorter from left to right. I also made a map of the route with the EQS scores written next to each site and shaded in different colours, where red is low and green is high.

I calculated the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for distance and EQS score, and got rs = 0.96. This is a very strong positive correlation. Using the table, the critical value for n = 10 is 0.65 at the 5% level, so the correlation is significant.

Analysis

The results show that the environmental quality does get better the further you go from the CBD. At Site 1, which was in the CBD, the EQS was 8 out of 30, while at Site 10, which was 4.3 km from the centre, the score was 26, so the score was more than three times higher. The scatter graph shows the points follow the line of best fit quite closely so there is a strong correlation. The Spearman's rank coefficient of 0.96 shows the same thing.

The traffic count was lower at the sites far from the CBD, from 112 at Site 1 to 33 at Site 10, and the noise level went from 78 dB to 57 dB. This helps to explain why the EQS was low in the centre. In the CBD there are lots of cars, buses and trams, so it is noisy and polluted. There was also a lot of litter and the buildings were old and some of them were empty. Further out there were more gardens, trees and houses that were in a better state, so the score was higher. For instance, at Site 9 and Site 10 there was a park and lots of trees.

There were a few anomalies. Site 3 has a lower score than Site 2 and Site 6 has a lower score than Site 5. At Site 6 there was a row of takeaway shops with lots of litter, which is probably the reason. At Site 3 there was a large construction site, which makes the area look worse. Site 8 also scored lower than Site 7, although only by 2.

This agrees with the Burgess model, which says that the environment should be best further out. It agrees with other studies that found that city centres have worse environmental quality because of traffic and pollution.

Conclusion

In conclusion, my hypothesis was correct. The environmental quality of Nottingham gets better as you move further away from the CBD. The null hypothesis can be rejected because the Spearman's rank result is above the critical value. This is probably because there is less traffic, less noise and more green space further from the centre.

Evaluation

There were some problems with the fieldwork. First, the EQS is subjective because it depends on what each person thinks, for example one person might think a building is in good condition and another might think it is not. We tried to reduce this by averaging the scores of four people, but there might still be bias. Second, the data was collected on one day only so the results might not be typical. For example, the traffic might be different on a weekday or on a weekend, and it was only counted for five minutes so I could not be sure that it was representative. It was also raining a bit during the afternoon so the litter might have looked worse. Third, I only used one transect, along one road, so my results can only really apply to the north of Nottingham and not to the whole city. Different parts of the city, for example the south by the river, might be different. Fourth, the sites were not evenly spaced because we ran out of time, which could have affected the line of best fit. Fifth, the noise meter was a phone app which is not as accurate as a proper decibel meter.

To make the investigation better I could have done more transects in different directions, collected data on different days, and had more people doing the survey. This would have given more reliable results.

Overall the fieldwork was a success because I answered my question and showed that the environmental quality is better further away from the CBD, which agrees with the Burgess model.

Bibliography
Burgess model (class notes)
Google Maps
Geography textbook

task: DP Business Management internal assessment (research project): To what extent has the introduction of a four-day working week improved employee motivation at a small digital marketing agency?
text:
To what extent has the introduction of a four-day working week improved employee motivation at Brightpath Digital, a small marketing agency in Manchester, and should the firm keep the policy?

Introduction and focus

Brightpath Digital is a private limited company in Manchester with 31 employees, founded in 2016, which provides social media management and search engine marketing to small and medium-sized firms. In January 2024 the owner and managing director introduced a four-day working week (Monday to Thursday) for all employees on the same salary, after a six-month trial. The decision is important to the firm because staff costs are its biggest expense (about 70% of revenue, according to the managing director) and because the agency competes with other firms for skilled graduates in a tight labour market. My research question requires evaluating motivation but also leads to a recommendation about whether the firm should continue, because that is what a manager would need to make a decision. I have access to the firm because the managing director is a family friend, and I agreed not to name individual employees.

The key concept of the investigation is change, the introduction of the four-day week as a strategic change in working practice, and the tools I use are motivation theories, the analysis of data using an adapted staff survey, and a stakeholder analysis. I decided to focus on motivation rather than productivity because motivation can be measured directly from employees' perceptions, whereas productivity in a creative agency is difficult to measure objectively.

Theoretical background

Motivation is the internal drive that causes employees to take action to achieve goals. I use two content theories. Herzberg's two-factor theory (1959) states that hygiene factors (pay, working conditions, job security, company policy) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate, while motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, the work itself, opportunity for growth) actually increase motivation. Maslow's hierarchy suggests that people move from physiological and safety needs to belonging, esteem and self-actualisation. A four-day week with unchanged pay could be seen as a hygiene factor (improved working conditions and work-life balance) and, by Herzberg's logic, would only reduce dissatisfaction, not directly motivate. But it might act as a motivator if employees see it as recognition of their trustworthiness and if the greater autonomy lets them take more responsibility for achieving the same output. I contrast this with Taylor's scientific management, which assumes workers are motivated mainly by pay; since the pay did not change, Taylor would predict no change in motivation. This provides a test: if motivation increased in spite of no pay increase, Herzberg's view that non-financial factors matter is supported.

Primary research

I carried out three kinds of primary research. (1) An anonymous online questionnaire with 18 statements on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) completed by 24 of the 31 employees (a 77% response rate), covering job satisfaction, energy at work, commitment, work-life balance and feelings of recognition. I asked respondents to answer both for "before the four-day week" and "now", and this retrospective design has weakness because people may not remember accurately, which I discuss below. (2) A semi-structured interview of 25 minutes with the managing director, Ms R (named with permission), about her reasons, the costs and the outcomes. (3) A short interview with two team leaders. I also used secondary data supplied by the firm: absence days and staff turnover over the previous 18 months, and the 4 Day Week Foundation's published reports on UK trials as a benchmark.

Primary research results

Table 1 (mean score out of 5 across 24 respondents, "before" and "now"):
"I feel motivated to do my best work": before 3.2, now 4.1
"I feel energetic at work": before 2.9, now 3.9
"I feel my employer recognises my contribution": before 3.1, now 3.6
"I feel I am given responsibility": before 3.5, now 3.7
"I have an acceptable work-life balance": before 2.6, now 4.5
"I intend to stay at the firm for the next two years": before 3.3, now 4.2
"I feel under pressure to complete my work in four days": not asked before, now 3.8

Figure 1: bar chart with paired bars (before and now) for each statement, showing the largest increase for work-life balance (+1.9) and the smallest for responsibility (+0.2). The stress statement has a single bar at 3.8.

Secondary data from the firm: absence days per employee fell from 6.2 in the year before to 3.8 in the 12 months after, and staff turnover fell from 22% to 9%. Ms R estimated that recruitment of each replaced employee had previously cost about £5,000. Revenue for the firm rose 6% during the period, but she said that this partly came from a new large client so it cannot be attributed to the four-day week.

Analysis

The data strongly suggest that motivation increased. The mean score for "I feel motivated to do my best work" increased from 3.2 to 4.1 (+0.9), and the energy score increased by 1.0. The largest change, work-life balance (from 2.6 to 4.5), is as expected, because it is the direct effect of a three-day weekend. Under Herzberg's theory, this is a hygiene factor, so the finding that general motivation also rose is notable. The smaller increases in "recognition" (+0.5) and "responsibility" (+0.2) suggest that real motivators changed less. A possible interpretation is that the four-day week works mainly by removing dissatisfaction and fatigue (which allows employees to perform better) rather than through new motivators, which fits Herzberg's classification and also Maslow's: stronger satisfaction of belonging and esteem needs outside work (more time with family and friends) may carry over to the workplace. The evidence also partly contradicts Taylor, since there was no pay rise but motivation rose, though it does not prove that pay is unimportant; the employees' pay was already considered adequate (one of the team leaders said no-one was currently underpaid).

The secondary data supports this: absence fell by 39% and turnover fell from 22% to 9%. If the avoided recruitment costs of about £5,000 are used, a fall from roughly 7 leavers to 3 per year (22% and 9% of 31) saves about £20,000 per year, though 31 staff is a small number so these figures are sensitive to chance. The standard deviation of responses was around 0.7 to 0.9, so the differences of 0.9 and 1.0 are larger than the typical spread, but I have not run a statistical test on only 24 paired responses.

The 3.8 score for "I feel under pressure to complete my work in four days" is a significant concern. One team leader said that deadlines had not changed, so the same work is done in 80% of the time, and she noticed that some staff work late in the evenings. This may reduce the long-term benefit: Herzberg's theory would say that excessive pressure is a hygiene problem that could cause dissatisfaction again. The managing director acknowledged that work intensity is a risk, particularly in the weeks before a campaign launch, and said that clients had occasionally been told that response would be slower on Fridays.

Evaluation of the evidence and the validity of the research

There are important limitations. First, the sample was small (24) and respondents were employees of one firm so the results cannot be generalised to other businesses; the findings are context-specific. Second, "before" scores were collected after the change, so they are likely to be affected by recall bias and by the "halo effect" that an employee who likes the new policy may remember the past as worse; a pre-trial survey would have been more reliable. Third, although the questionnaire was anonymous, employees may have exaggerated their positive responses because the policy is valued and they want to keep it (social desirability bias). Fourth, the interview with the managing director might be biased, as she has a personal interest in showing that her decision worked. The turnover and absence figures come from the firm's own records so are likely to be accurate but involve small numbers, and other factors (a hot labour market, a new office, a bonus in 2023) could have contributed. Finally, I do not have a control group, so I cannot separate the effect of the policy from a "novelty" effect, which might fade; the trial is only 12 months old.

Conclusion and recommendation

To a large extent the four-day week has improved the motivation of employees at Brightpath: self-reported motivation and energy rose by about one point on a five-point scale, and intention to stay, absence and turnover all moved in a positive direction. However, the improvement is mainly the result of better work-life balance rather than increased recognition or responsibility, and a significant number of staff feel under pressure. I therefore recommend that Brightpath should keep the four-day week, but should (1) review workloads and client deadlines so that the pressure is not simply moved to evenings, (2) use the greater employee goodwill to introduce genuine motivators such as team-based targets, training and recognition schemes to follow Herzberg's advice, and (3) repeat the survey in 12 months with a before-and-after design to see if the effect lasts. The decision should be reviewed if client satisfaction falls.

Bibliography
Herzberg, F. (1959) The Motivation to Work. New York: Wiley.
Maslow, A. (1943) A theory of human motivation. Psychological Review, 50(4).
Taylor, F.W. (1911) The Principles of Scientific Management.
4 Day Week Foundation (2023) The UK pilot results.
Brightpath Digital staff survey and company records (2024); interview with managing director, 3 March 2024.

task: DP Business Management internal assessment (research project): Should Kaleidoscope Cafe open a second branch in order to grow its profits?
text:
Should Kaleidoscope Cafe open a second branch?

1. Introduction

Kaleidoscope Cafe is a small independent cafe in the centre of Leeds, owned by a husband and wife, which has been open for six years. It sells coffee, cakes, brunch and sandwiches to students and office workers. The cafe is very popular and is often full at lunch times and on weekends, with queues out the door. The owners are thinking about expanding by opening a second branch. I chose this business because my aunt is one of the owners, so I was able to get information from them. I think it is a good topic because growth is something that all businesses think about at some time and it will help me to understand more about business strategy and how decisions are made. I also like cafes.

My research question is: Should Kaleidoscope Cafe open a second branch?

The aim of this research is to analyse whether the cafe should open a second branch, which would be about 3 miles away in the suburb of Headingley, near the university, and to recommend a course of action.

2. Background information

Kaleidoscope Cafe is a sole proprietorship, so the owners have unlimited liability. It has 9 employees, 4 full time and 5 part time, and it makes about £260,000 in revenue each year. The owners say the profit is about £38,000 a year. The cafe has a strong brand because of its colourful interior, its specialty coffee and its Instagram account which has 12,000 followers. The business is in the service sector and it is in the tertiary sector of the economy. The cafe's main competitors are Starbucks, Costa and other independent cafes in the area. The target market is young people aged 18 to 35, who are mostly students and young professionals.

The owners have said that they have enough money saved to open the second branch but that they would also need a loan of about £45,000 from the bank. The second branch would need to be rented, renovated and equipped, and staff would have to be hired.

3. Theory

Growth is when a business increases in size. There are two types of growth: internal (organic) growth, where a business grows from within, for example by opening new branches or launching new products, and external growth, where a business grows by merging with or taking over another business. Opening a second branch is internal growth. Reasons for growth are to make more profit, to gain economies of scale, to get a bigger share of the market, and to reduce risks by diversifying. Economies of scale are the advantages of large-scale production that lead to lower unit costs, for example buying coffee beans in bulk at a discount. However there can also be diseconomies of scale, such as poor communication and lower motivation of workers when the business gets too large.

I will also use SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) to evaluate the cafe, and investment appraisal using payback period and average rate of return (ARR). The payback period is the length of time it takes to recover the initial investment. ARR is the average annual profit divided by the initial investment, as a percentage. Decision-making can also be done with a decision tree. Ansoff's matrix is a model that shows four ways to grow: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification. Opening a second branch in a new area is market development, because the existing product is sold in a new market, which is of medium risk.

Kaleidoscope Cafe has a tall organisational structure for such a small business, with the two owners at the top, one manager, two baristas who lead the shifts, and then the other staff. Decisions are made by the owners, which is an autocratic style, though my aunt said that they ask for suggestions from staff when they are deciding on new menu items. Employees are paid slightly above the minimum wage and the owners give them a share of tips. Staff motivation is quite high, although my aunt said that two baristas have left in the last year to work in bigger chains. The cafe buys its coffee beans from a local roaster in Leeds, which is a bit more expensive than the beans that big chains use, but customers can taste the difference and the owners think it is a unique selling point. Most of the cafe's sales come from hot drinks (about 55%), then food (35%) and cold drinks and other items (10%). The gross profit margin on hot drinks is about 70% but only about 45% on food because the ingredients cost more.

The cafe's break-even point is about 4,200 customers per month according to my aunt. At the moment it has about 7,500 customers per month, so the margin of safety is quite large. If a second cafe had half this number of customers it would be roughly at the break-even point after its fixed costs of rent (about £2,400 per month), staff and utilities. These numbers are approximate and I was not shown the accounts, only told them in the interview.

The business also has to think about its stakeholders. The owners and employees are internal stakeholders, while customers, suppliers, the landlord and the bank are external. A second branch would affect all of them, for example the roaster would sell more beans but the staff might have to work at both cafes.

4. Primary research

I carried out primary research using a survey and an interview. I interviewed my aunt, who is one of the owners, for about 20 minutes, and asked her about the cafe's finances and about the plans. I also conducted a survey of 30 customers of the cafe using a paper questionnaire handed out on a Saturday afternoon. I asked 6 questions, including how often they visit, whether they would visit a second branch, and what they like about the cafe. I picked the customers who were sitting in the cafe, and I chose them by asking people who looked friendly.

Results of the customer survey:
Of the 30 customers, 22 (73%) said they visit at least once a week.
18 (60%) said that they live or work close to the current cafe.
9 (30%) said they would visit a second branch in Headingley.
When asked what they like most: coffee quality 12, atmosphere 10, friendly staff 6, other 2.
Figure 1: pie chart showing the reasons customers like the cafe, with coffee quality at 40% and atmosphere at 33%.

The owners gave me the following estimates for the second branch: set-up cost £85,000 (including renovation, equipment and deposit), expected profit in year 1 £6,000, year 2 £18,000, year 3 £26,000, year 4 £30,000 and year 5 £32,000.

5. Analysis

SWOT analysis of Kaleidoscope Cafe:
Strengths: strong brand and loyal customers, high quality of coffee, good location, an active Instagram account.
Weaknesses: small business with limited funds, the owners have no experience of running more than one site, and dependence on the owners.
Opportunities: more students in Headingley and a growing demand for specialty coffee and brunch.
Threats: competition from big chains and other independents, rising rents and costs of ingredients, and the risk that the quality will fall in the second cafe.

Investment appraisal: the total profit over five years is 6,000 + 18,000 + 26,000 + 30,000 + 32,000 = £112,000. The average annual profit is £22,400. The ARR is 22,400 / 85,000 x 100 = 26.4%. For the payback, the cumulative profits are £6,000 after year 1, £24,000 after year 2, £50,000 after year 3, £80,000 after year 4 and £112,000 after year 5, so the investment of £85,000 would be paid back in about 4.2 years (4 years plus 5,000/32,000 = 0.16 years). This is quite a long time for a small business, but the ARR of 26.4% is quite good compared with a bank savings rate of about 4%.

Customer survey analysis: only 30% of the customers said they would visit the second branch, but this is because most of them live near the current cafe, so it is not surprising. The second branch would be in a different area so it would get different customers. The survey shows that customers like the coffee quality and atmosphere, so as long as the second branch copies these things, it should do well.

Ansoff's matrix: opening in a new area is market development, which is medium risk.

Growth by opening a second branch could give economies of scale because the owners could buy ingredients in larger amounts and share the cost of marketing, such as the Instagram account. On the other hand, the owners would be spending time at the second branch, and the first branch might suffer. There might be diseconomies of scale because it is more difficult to maintain the same quality.

6. Evaluation

The research has some limitations. The sample size of 30 customers is small and the customers were all current customers, who are more likely to be positive, so the survey is biased. I also chose them by asking people who looked friendly, which is a convenience sample. The profit forecasts are estimates provided by the owners and may be too optimistic, because they want to expand. I also only interviewed one of the owners, and it was my aunt, so she might have given me the answers that she thought I wanted. Finally, I did not research the competitors in Headingley or the rents there, so I do not know whether the forecasts are realistic.

7. Conclusion and recommendation

In conclusion, I think that Kaleidoscope Cafe should open a second branch. The investment appraisal gives an ARR of 26.4% and a payback of about 4.2 years, and the cafe has strengths such as a loyal customer base and a strong brand. Although there are risks, such as the loan and the possible fall in quality, I think that the benefits outweigh them. However, the owners should do more research about Headingley before they make a final decision, and they should consider changing to a limited company to reduce the personal risk. They could also try a pop-up cafe in Headingley first to test the market.
